rv.q: This treat of a play leaves its characters, not to mention its audience, asking themselves some long, hard questions.
It feels somehow distant and etiolated on the wide stage of the Lyttelton Theatre; the pacing goes awry in places and some plot twists become muffled.
There’s an authentic, rare flavour to this story, too – but it’ll take an experienced palate to fully appreciate it.
Now it seems a quainter museum piece, though the essential story remains a brilliant idea.
But it seems old-fashioned in this faithfully period production.
It is a real shame, then, that the production feels so tonally muddled.
Yet the inaudibility of much of Synge’s poetry is a major stumbling block – and the issue should have been resolved during rehearsal by the National itself.
Eye-catching, yes, but not quite enough to make the drama seem more than a mildly intriguing period piece.
It’s a brilliant and satisfying production that will leave audiences thinking long after the show ends.
A piece of music, in three acts or movements, played by a brilliant ensemble with vivacity, rhythm, fine timing and tone.

A sharp and rich production, The Playboy of the Western World’s ridicule of reductively romantic veneration of causes or cultures is more relevant than ever and should provoke as much thought as it entertains.
It entertains, but the pacing is slightly too slow for it to be full-on engaging.

It’s impressive but dramatically inert, ultimately not really proving why Synge’s tale of romantic disappointment and the ludicrousness of putting people on a pedestal, is worthy of a major revival at the present time.
You may be glad you went but you’ll certainly be glad to get out.
All of these versions of the play never quite gel, and for those new to the play, it may be hard to grasp who everyone is and what they want.
But this production is too colorfully spectacular for this particular drama.

cn.t: Synge's Irish classic receives a mixed reception, with praise for its operatic staging and Coughlan's star presence, but criticism for unclear tonal direction and dialect difficulties that leave the production feeling uneven.
